title: Inherited Diseases of the Liver, Pancreas, and Colon
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the single-gene diseases that most often injure the digestive organs: iron overload in hereditary hemochromatosis, copper overload in Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, the two molecular routes to colorectal cancer with their inherited syndromes, and the gut and liver effects of cystic fibrosis. Board questions either name a gene or inheritance pattern and ask what follows, or describe skin, eye, joint, lung, or stool findings and ask for the gene. Each section traces one molecular defect from the normal protein to every finding it explains.
prerequisites: Mendelian inheritance patterns, codominance, penetrance, and the Knudson two-hit model
Protein folding, endoplasmic reticulum quality control, and proteasomal degradation
Liver acinus zones and biliary excretion (GI-9)
Exocrine pancreatic secretion and fat digestion (GI-6, GI-7)
Oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair

connections.how: Metal overload and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency are inherited causes of chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
The adenoma to carcinoma and mismatch repair pathways explain the behavior, location, and histology of sporadic and inherited colorectal cancers.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and cystic fibrosis damage the lung through the same proteins that injure the liver and pancreas.
Hepcidin and ferroportin control both dietary iron absorption and macrophage iron recycling, and free copper causes hemolysis in Wilson disease.
Cystic fibrosis is the classic inherited cause of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

sections.title: Hereditary hemochromatosis: low hepcidin and parenchymal iron overload

blocks.text: The body has no regulated way to excrete iron. Adults lose only about 1 to 2 mg per day in shed cells and minor bleeding, so total body iron (about 3 to 4 g) is controlled at absorption. The controller is hepcidin, a peptide hormone made by hepatocytes. Hepcidin binds ferroportin on duodenal enterocytes and macrophages and causes its internalization and degradation. Low hepcidin therefore lets iron flow into plasma.

Hepatocytes raise hepcidin when transferrin saturation rises. HFE, an MHC class I-like protein that must pair with beta-2 microglobulin to reach the cell surface, works with transferrin receptors and the BMP6 to SMAD signaling pathway to turn on the hepcidin gene. Hereditary hemochromatosis (HH) is most often caused by homozygosity for the HFE C282Y mutation on chromosome 6p, inherited as an autosomal recessive trait and common in people of Northern European descent. Replacing cysteine 282 with tyrosine breaks a disulfide bond, so HFE cannot bind beta-2 microglobulin and stays inside the cell. The liver therefore makes too little hepcidin for the body's iron stores, and the gut keeps absorbing iron as though the person were iron deficient.

blocks.title: From HFE mutation to organ injury
steps: Homozygous HFE C282Y impairs hepatocyte iron sensing
Hepcidin stays inappropriately low
Ferroportin stays active on enterocytes and macrophages
Excess iron absorbed and released into plasma for years
Transferrin saturates; non-transferrin-bound iron enters parenchymal cells
Fenton reaction makes hydroxyl radicals
Lipid peroxidation, cell death, and stellate cell fibrosis
blocks.caption: HH is a hormone deficiency: the defect is the hepcidin signal, not the iron transporters themselves.

blocks.text: Once transferrin is saturated, non-transferrin-bound iron enters parenchymal cells of the liver, pancreas, heart, joints, and pituitary. Free ferrous iron drives the Fenton reaction (Fe2+ plus hydrogen peroxide yields the hydroxyl radical), which peroxidizes membranes, damages mitochondria and DNA, and activates hepatic stellate cells to lay down collagen. Iron appears first as hemosiderin in periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes and stains blue with Prussian blue. Because ferroportin stays active, macrophages in spleen and marrow hold relatively little iron, the reverse of transfusional overload, in which iron is delivered to macrophages first.

blocks.title: Organ damage in hereditary hemochromatosis
rows: Hepatocyte oxidative injury and stellate cell fibrosis
Iron injury to beta cells, plus insulin resistance from liver disease
Increased melanin, with some dermal hemosiderin
Dilated (sometimes restrictive) cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, conduction block
Synovial iron and calcium pyrophosphate deposition
Arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, chondrocalcinosis
blocks.caption: Cirrhosis, diabetes, and skin pigmentation form the classic triad sometimes called bronze diabetes.

blocks.text: Disease usually appears in middle age, after total body iron has reached many times normal. Women present about a decade later than men because menstruation and pregnancy remove iron. Penetrance is incomplete: many C282Y homozygotes have high iron studies but no organ damage; alcohol, viral hepatitis, and modifier genes push some toward cirrhosis. The laboratory signature is a high transferrin saturation (above about 45%), the earliest marker, with a high ferritin that reflects stored iron. Cirrhosis greatly raises the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma because hepatocytes regenerate for years under oxidative DNA damage. Iron-rich tissue also favors siderophilic bacteria such as Vibrio vulnificus, Yersinia enterocolitica, and Listeria monocytogenes.

blocks.predict: A man with beta-thalassemia major who receives regular transfusions develops iron overload. Where does the iron first accumulate, and how does that differ from HFE hemochromatosis?
blocks.explain: Transfused red cells are removed by macrophages, so iron loads the reticuloendothelial system first; in HH, low hepcidin keeps macrophages exporting iron, so parenchymal cells load first.

sections.title: Wilson disease: failed copper excretion and ceruloplasmin loading

blocks.text: Copper is a cofactor for cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase, and ceruloplasmin, but free copper is a strong oxidant. Where iron balance is set at absorption, copper balance is set at excretion: bile is the only significant route for removing excess copper. Inside the hepatocyte, the chaperone ATOX1 delivers copper to ATP7B, a P-type copper-transporting ATPase in the trans-Golgi network. ATP7B has two jobs. It pumps copper into the Golgi lumen, where it is built into apoceruloplasmin to form ceruloplasmin, and when hepatocyte copper rises it moves to vesicles near the canalicular membrane and sends copper into bile.

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is the autosomal recessive loss of ATP7B, encoded on chromosome 13q. Both jobs fail. Apoceruloplasmin is secreted without copper, is unstable, and is degraded quickly, so serum ceruloplasmin is low. Copper cannot enter bile, so it accumulates in hepatocytes, first bound to metallothionein and then free, where it generates reactive oxygen species, injures mitochondria, and produces steatosis, chronic hepatitis, and eventually cirrhosis. When hepatocyte storage is exceeded or hepatocytes die, copper that is not bound to ceruloplasmin spills into blood and deposits in other tissues.

blocks.title: Copper accumulation in Wilson disease
steps: Biallelic ATP7B loss in hepatocytes
No copper loading onto ceruloplasmin; no biliary copper excretion
Low serum ceruloplasmin; copper builds up in the liver
Oxidative hepatocyte injury: steatosis, hepatitis, cirrhosis
Free copper released into blood
Deposits in cornea, basal ganglia, kidney; red cells hemolyze
blocks.caption: The liver is injured first; the eye, brain, and kidney are injured by copper that overflows from it.

blocks.title: Wilson disease findings and their mechanisms

Ceruloplasmin normally carries most plasma copper; the unbound fraction rises
Unbound copper is filtered by the glomerulus

Copper cannot leave the hepatocyte in bile
Copper in Descemet membrane at the corneal periphery
Tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, parkinsonism, psychiatric change
Copper injury to the lenticular nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus)

blocks.caption: Total body copper is high even though serum ceruloplasmin and total serum copper are low.

blocks.text: Presentation depends on age. Children and adolescents usually present with liver disease, ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis. Young adults more often present with movement disorders or psychiatric change, because copper has had time to reach the brain. Kayser-Fleischer rings are found in nearly all patients with neurologic disease but in only about half of those with liver disease alone, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

Two distinctions matter. Ceruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation can raise it into the normal range, and it is also low in protein-losing states, severe liver failure of any cause, and some heterozygous carriers; no single value is diagnostic. Menkes disease is the mirror image: X-linked loss of ATP7A, the enterocyte copper exporter, blocks absorption and causes copper deficiency with kinky hair, connective tissue weakness, and neurodegeneration.

sections.title: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: a toxic protein in the liver and too little in the lung

blocks.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) encoded by SERPINA1 on chromosome 14q. Hepatocytes make most of it and secrete it into plasma, where it forms the major part of the alpha-1 globulin band on serum protein electrophoresis. Its main target is neutrophil elastase in the lung. AAT acts as bait: elastase cleaves its reactive center loop, the inhibitor changes shape, and the enzyme is trapped in an inactive complex. Alleles are codominant and named by electrophoretic mobility: M is normal, S is mildly deficient, Z is severely deficient, and null alleles make no protein.

The Z allele (Glu342Lys) destabilizes the protein during folding. The reactive loop of one Z molecule inserts into the beta-sheet of the next, a process called loop-sheet polymerization, and the chains cannot leave the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Most Z protein is retained, so PiZZ homozygotes have serum levels of only about 10 to 15% of normal. One mutation therefore causes two different diseases by two different mechanisms.

blocks.title: One mutation, two mechanisms
steps: SERPINA1 Z allele (Glu342Lys) misfolds
Z protein polymerizes in the hepatocyte ER
Liver: retained polymers cause ER stress and hepatocyte death
Regeneration and fibrosis lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
Lung: little AAT reaches plasma and alveoli
Unopposed neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls
Panacinar emphysema, worst at the lung bases
blocks.caption: Liver disease is a toxic gain of function; lung disease is a loss of function.

blocks.text: In the liver, retained polymers trigger ER stress, mitochondrial injury, and apoptosis, and the surviving hepatocytes regenerate under chronic injury, which leads to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. The polymers appear as round eosinophilic globules in periportal hepatocytes that are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. PAS stains carbohydrate, and diastase digests glycogen; a glycoprotein such as AAT keeps its PAS stain after diastase, which separates these globules from glycogen. Liver disease can appear as neonatal cholestatic hepatitis in a minority of PiZZ infants or as cirrhosis in adults, and its severity varies with how efficiently each person degrades the retained polymers.

In the lung, too little AAT leaves neutrophil elastase free to digest elastin. Damage involves the whole acinus (panacinar emphysema) and is worst in the lower lobes, probably because they receive more blood flow and therefore more neutrophils. This differs from smoking-related centriacinar emphysema, which favors the upper lobes. Smoking accelerates AAT deficiency greatly: oxidants convert methionine 358 in the reactive loop to methionine sulfoxide, inactivating the remaining inhibitor, and smoke recruits more neutrophils. Smokers with PiZZ often develop emphysema in their 30s or 40s.

blocks.title: Predicting disease from genotype
blocks.text: Compare three genotypes. PiZZ: about 10 to 15% of normal serum AAT, with polymers retained in hepatocytes, so both cirrhosis and emphysema are possible. Null/null: no AAT is made at all, so serum levels are lowest and emphysema is severe, but nothing accumulates in the ER, so the liver is spared. PiMZ: the M allele is secreted normally and the Z allele is partly retained, giving intermediate serum levels (roughly half to two-thirds of normal) with little lung risk in nonsmokers and only a modestly raised risk of liver disease when another insult is present. The rule that follows: liver disease requires a retained, misfolded protein, while lung disease requires only a low serum level.

sections.title: Two molecular pathways to colorectal cancer

blocks.text: Colonic epithelium renews every few days from stem cells at the crypt base, where Wnt signaling keeps cells proliferating. As cells move up the crypt, Wnt signaling falls and beta-catenin, the transcriptional effector of the pathway, is destroyed by a complex that includes APC, axin, and glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta. This complex phosphorylates beta-catenin and marks it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, so surface cells stop dividing.
Chromosomal instability: the adenoma to carcinoma sequence

Most sporadic colorectal cancers follow this route. Loss of both APC alleles (chromosome 5q) is the gatekeeping event: beta-catenin escapes destruction, enters the nucleus, and with TCF transcription factors switches on growth genes such as MYC and cyclin D1, producing a small adenoma. An activating KRAS point mutation, which needs only one allele, impairs GTP hydrolysis, holding the GTPase in its active GTP-bound state and giving growth-factor-independent signaling, so the adenoma enlarges. Loss of chromosome 18q genes such as SMAD4 removes growth inhibition by TGF-beta. Loss of TP53 (chromosome 17p) comes late: without p53, cells with DNA damage neither arrest in G1 nor undergo apoptosis, and the adenoma becomes an invasive carcinoma. The order is typical rather than fixed; the accumulation of hits matters most, and the sequence usually takes about a decade.

blocks.title: Adenoma to carcinoma sequence
steps: Normal colonic mucosa
APC loss: beta-catenin accumulates, early adenoma
KRAS activation: adenoma enlarges
SMAD4 and other 18q losses
TP53 loss: no G1 arrest or apoptosis
Invasive adenocarcinoma
blocks.caption: Tumor suppressors (APC, SMAD4, TP53) need two hits; the oncogene KRAS needs one.

blocks.text: Microsatellite instability and Lynch syndrome

DNA polymerase slips on microsatellites, short tandem repeats such as runs of CA, creating small insertion or deletion loops. Mismatch repair proteins correct these errors: MSH2 with MSH6 recognizes the mismatch, and MLH1 with PMS2 directs excision and resynthesis. When repair fails, repeat lengths change throughout the genome, producing microsatellite instability (MSI) and frameshift mutations in growth genes that contain repeats, such as TGFBR2 and BAX. Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) is an autosomal dominant germline mutation in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 (or an EPCAM deletion that silences MSH2). The germline mutation is the first hit, and a somatic second hit in any cell removes repair. Patients have few adenomas, but each progresses quickly, so cancers appear early (often in the 40s). Endometrial cancer is the most common extracolonic tumor, followed by ovarian, gastric, small bowel, urothelial, and hepatobiliary cancers. Most MSI colorectal cancers, however, are sporadic and arise when the MLH1 promoter is silenced by hypermethylation, usually in serrated lesions with BRAF V600E mutations.

blocks.title: Comparing the two pathways
rows: About 15%; Lynch syndrome is a small fraction
Aneuploid, gains and losses of chromosomes
Mucinous or poorly differentiated, many lymphocytes
blocks.caption: Both pathways end in adenocarcinoma, but they differ in genes, genome pattern, location, and histology.

blocks.title: Is this MSI tumor inherited or sporadic?
blocks.text: A right-sided colon cancer shows microsatellite instability and, on immunohistochemistry, loss of MLH1 and PMS2 staining. PMS2 is lost too because PMS2 is unstable without its partner MLH1, so the primary defect is MLH1. MLH1 loss can be germline (Lynch) or sporadic (promoter hypermethylation). If the tumor carries BRAF V600E and the MLH1 promoter is methylated, the pattern fits the sporadic serrated pathway. If neither is present, a germline MLH1 mutation is likely. Loss of MSH2 with MSH6, by contrast, points to a germline MSH2 (or EPCAM) defect.

Polyposis syndromes are distinguished by the gene involved, the inheritance pattern, and above all the type of polyp. An adenoma is a dysplastic neoplasm of the glandular epithelium and is itself a precursor of carcinoma. A hamartoma is a disorganized overgrowth of normal tissue elements; it is not dysplastic, yet the syndromes that produce hamartomas still raise cancer risk.

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant germline mutation in APC on chromosome 5q, with about a quarter of cases arising de novo. Every colonic cell already carries one mutant allele, so a single somatic hit in any crypt starts an adenoma. That explains why hundreds to thousands of adenomas carpet the colon from adolescence and why colorectal cancer is nearly certain by about age 40 to 50 if the colon remains. Duodenal and periampullary adenomas and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium are also common. Attenuated FAP, from mutations at the ends of the gene, produces fewer than 100 adenomas and later cancer.

Gardner syndrome is FAP with prominent extracolonic growths: osteomas of the skull and mandible, desmoid tumors, epidermoid cysts, and dental anomalies such as supernumerary or impacted teeth. Turcot syndrome is colorectal polyposis with a primary brain tumor; medulloblastoma accompanies APC mutations, and glioblastoma accompanies mismatch repair defects.

MUTYH-associated polyposis is autosomal recessive. Oxidized guanine (8-oxoguanine) pairs with adenine during replication, and the MUTYH glycosylase removes that adenine as part of base excision repair. Without both copies of MUTYH, G:C to T:A transversions accumulate, including in APC and KRAS, producing tens to a few hundred adenomas and a high cancer risk. Because both alleles must be lost, parents are usually unaffected carriers and siblings share the risk.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is autosomal dominant loss of STK11 (LKB1), a kinase that activates AMP-activated protein kinase and so restrains mTOR-driven growth. Hamartomatous polyps occur mainly in the small intestine and have a characteristic branching core of smooth muscle covered by normal mucosa. Large polyps lead the bowel into intussusception or bleed. Melanin pigmentation appears in childhood on the lips, buccal mucosa, and skin of the hands and feet. Cancer risk rises in the colon, stomach, small bowel, pancreas, breast, ovary, and testis.

blocks.title: Inherited polyposis syndromes
rows: Near-certain colorectal cancer; retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy
Osteomas, desmoids, epidermoid cysts, extra teeth
Base excision repair defect; unaffected parents
Mucocutaneous pigmentation, intussusception, many cancer sites
blocks.caption: Lynch syndrome is not a polyposis syndrome: it produces few adenomas (see C04).

blocks.predict: A 45-year-old has about 60 colonic adenomas. Neither parent had polyps, but his sister has a similar number. Which syndrome fits best?
blocks.explain: MUTYH-associated polyposis: an attenuated adenoma count with affected siblings and unaffected parents fits autosomal recessive inheritance, whereas FAP is dominant.

sections.title: Cystic fibrosis in the gut, pancreas, and liver

blocks.text: CFTR, encoded on chromosome 7q, is an ATP-binding cassette protein that works as an anion channel. Protein kinase A, activated by cAMP, phosphorylates its regulatory domain, and ATP binding at its nucleotide-binding domains opens the pore to chloride and bicarbonate. In secretory epithelia (pancreatic ducts, cholangiocytes, intestinal crypts, and airways), apical anion secretion draws sodium across the tight junctions and water follows, keeping secretions fluid. In pancreatic ducts, CFTR also supports chloride and bicarbonate exchange that produces the bicarbonate-rich juice that neutralizes gastric acid.

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is autosomal recessive and most common in people of Northern European descent, with a carrier frequency of about 1 in 25. The most common mutation, F508del, removes a phenylalanine and causes misfolding; ER quality control sends the protein for proteasomal degradation, so little CFTR reaches the apical membrane. Other mutation classes block synthesis (nonsense mutations), gating, or conductance, but all reduce anion and water secretion, leaving secretions thick, dehydrated, and acidic.

blocks.title: From CFTR mutation to fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
steps: F508del CFTR misfolds and is degraded
Little CFTR at the apical duct membrane
Chloride and bicarbonate secretion fall; less water follows
Thick, acidic secretions plug pancreatic ductules
Acini are destroyed and replaced by fibrosis and fat
Lipase deficit causes steatorrhea
Vitamin A, D, E, and K malabsorption
blocks.caption: Pancreatic destruction begins before birth, so most patients have exocrine insufficiency from infancy.

blocks.title: Gastrointestinal effects of cystic fibrosis
rows: Dehydrated, protein-rich meconium sticks to the mucosa
Meconium ileus at birth; perforation can cause meconium peritonitis
Steatorrhea, failure to thrive, high immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening
Low bicarbonate leaves the pH low, inactivating enzymes and precipitating bile acids
Islets damaged later by surrounding fibrosis
CF-related diabetes in adolescence and adulthood
Thick bile plugs ductules, causing local inflammation and fibrosis
Focal biliary cirrhosis; in a minority, multilobular cirrhosis with portal hypertension
blocks.caption: Every lesion traces back to too little water in a secretion that depends on CFTR.

blocks.text: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency follows directly from fat malabsorption, because vitamins A, D, E, and K are absorbed within micelles with dietary fat. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia; vitamin D deficiency causes rickets or osteomalacia; vitamin E deficiency causes hemolytic anemia and a spinocerebellar neuropathy; vitamin K deficiency lowers factors II, VII, IX, and X and prolongs the prothrombin time. Protein malabsorption can cause hypoalbuminemia and edema in infants.

The sweat duct shows CFTR working in the opposite direction. There it reabsorbs chloride from the lumen, and sodium follows, so normal sweat reaching the skin is dilute. Without CFTR, chloride and sodium stay in the duct and sweat is salty; a sweat chloride of about 60 mmol/L or more supports the diagnosis. The same channel defect explains the lung disease, and congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens causes male infertility.

blocks.predict: Why is sweat chloride high in CF when the defect reduces chloride movement in both the pancreas and the sweat duct?
blocks.explain: In the pancreatic duct CFTR secretes chloride into the lumen, but in the sweat duct it reabsorbs chloride from the lumen; losing reabsorption leaves chloride in the sweat.
blocks.check: Compare with the first and last paragraphs of this section.

integration.text: These diseases share a logic that crosses disciplines. Biochemistry defines the faulty protein: a hormone signal (HFE and hepcidin), a metal pump (ATP7B), a misfolded inhibitor (AAT), a degradation complex or repair enzyme (APC, mismatch repair, MUTYH), or an ion channel (CFTR). Cell biology then decides the kind of injury. Misfolding in the ER produces toxic retention in AAT deficiency but degradation and loss of function with F508del CFTR, and free iron and copper injure through the same oxidant chemistry. Anatomy and histology explain where damage appears: periportal hepatocytes, the lenticular nucleus, Descemet membrane, pancreatic ductules, and colonic crypts.

Genetics predicts who is affected and how quickly. Recessive loss-of-function diseases (HH, Wilson, CF, MUTYH) require two mutant germline alleles; dominant cancer syndromes (FAP, Lynch, Peutz-Jeghers) carry one hit in every cell, so one somatic event starts a tumor. Codominance explains the graded AAT levels, and incomplete penetrance in HH shows that genotype alone does not guarantee disease. Pathology links these defects to common clinical pictures (cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, emphysema, malabsorption, and colon cancer) that also arise from nongenetic causes, so the gene must be inferred from the full pattern of findings.

summary: HFE C282Y hemochromatosis is autosomal recessive; low hepcidin leaves ferroportin active, so iron absorption continues despite overload.
Free iron injures parenchymal cells by the Fenton reaction, causing cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, diabetes, skin pigmentation, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, and hypogonadism.
Wilson disease is autosomal recessive ATP7B loss: copper is neither loaded onto ceruloplasmin nor excreted in bile, so ceruloplasmin is low while body copper is high.
Overflow copper produces Kayser-Fleischer rings, basal ganglia degeneration, Coombs-negative hemolysis, and high urinary copper.
PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin polymerizes in the hepatocyte ER, forming PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules and cirrhosis, while low serum levels cause lower-lobe panacinar emphysema.
The chromosomal instability pathway proceeds through APC loss, KRAS activation, and TP53 loss; FAP is its germline form.
Mismatch repair failure causes microsatellite instability; Lynch syndrome is the autosomal dominant germline form, while most sporadic MSI cancers come from MLH1 promoter methylation.
FAP (autosomal dominant APC) produces hundreds of adenomas; MUTYH polyposis is autosomal recessive; Peutz-Jeghers (STK11) produces hamartomas with mucocutaneous pigmentation.
CFTR loss reduces chloride, bicarbonate, and water secretion, causing meconium ileus, pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea and vitamin A, D, E, and K deficiency, and focal biliary cirrhosis.
